relationship: parallel warning against human reliance in place of hope in God
rationale: Jeremiah curses reliance on a human when the heart departs from the Lord; the psalm warns against trusting rulers and human beings who cannot save, then blesses hope in God. The contrast concerns the object of trust, not a ban on every human relationship.

relationship: same-chapter contrast between desolate and well-watered plants
rationale: The person relying on a human is compared to a wild tamarisk in an uninhabited salt wilderness. The following blessing compares the person trusting the Lord to a tree rooted beside water and continuing to bear fruit, forming the oracle's deliberate botanical contrast.

relationship: close blessing of the person whose hope is the Lord
rationale: Both explicitly pronounce blessing or happiness upon a person whose hope is in the Lord. The psalm further calls the God of Jacob that person's Helper.

relationship: close image of the fruitful tree beside water
rationale: Both portray a favored person as a tree beside water that continues to bear fruit. Jeremiah expressly addresses heat and a rainless year; the psalm adds an unfailing leaf and prosperity in the person's actions.

relationship: related depth of the human heart and difficulty of knowing it
rationale: Jeremiah calls the heart deep and asks who will know the human being; Proverbs compares counsel in a person's heart to deep water that an intelligent person draws out. The comparison preserves depth and discernment without importing a claim that Jeremiah calls the heart deceitful.

relationship: close divine testing of hearts and kidneys
rationale: Jeremiah names the Lord as examiner of hearts and tester of kidneys; the psalm addresses God with the same paired inward testing. Both place that examination in a setting of distinguishing righteous and wicked conduct.

relationship: close repayment according to each person's deeds
rationale: Jeremiah says the Lord gives each person according to his ways and the fruits of his practices; Romans says God repays each according to his works. This target supplies the explicit recompense clause, distinct from the heart-and-kidney imagery.

relationship: related adverse outcomes of unjustly acquired wealth
rationale: Jeremiah joins wealth made without judgment to abandonment in the middle of the possessor's days and final foolishness; Proverbs says property pursued with lawlessness diminishes. Proverbs does not reproduce the partridge image or Jeremiah's timing in the middle of the person's days.

relationship: related sanctuary as the place of God's throne
rationale: Jeremiah calls the sanctuary an exalted throne of glory. In Ezekiel's temple vision, God identifies the place of His throne and the footprints of His feet where His name will dwell among Israel.

relationship: close accusation of abandoning the divine fountain of life
rationale: Both passages condemn abandoning the Lord under the image of life-giving water. Jeremiah 2 develops the contrast with broken cisterns, whereas Jeremiah 17 asks shame upon those abandoning Him.

relationship: parallel appeal to the Lord for healing and salvation
rationale: Jeremiah asks the Lord to heal and save him; the psalm likewise asks divine healing and rescue. Jeremiah grounds the appeal in the Lord as his boast, while the psalm appeals to mercy amid bodily and inward distress.

relationship: close challenge that the announced divine action should arrive
rationale: Jeremiah reports people asking where the Lord's word is and demanding that it come. Isaiah reports a comparable challenge that God's action and the Holy One's counsel should approach so the challengers can see and know.

relationship: related appeal to God's knowledge of the speaker
rationale: Jeremiah appeals to the Lord's knowledge and places what proceeds from his lips before Him. The psalm speaks of divine testing and knowledge of the speaker's movements and reasonings, then mentions the tongue and God's knowledge of all things; it does not explain Jeremiah's unusual phrase about a human's day.

relationship: parallel plea against divine estrangement during danger
rationale: Jeremiah asks that the Lord not become an estrangement to him in an evil day. The psalm asks God not to forsake or remain far from the speaker while enemies plot against him.

relationship: parallel appeal for shame and reversal upon pursuers
rationale: Both ask that those pursuing or seeking the speaker's life be shamed and overtaken by judgment. Jeremiah asks double crushing; the psalm develops reversal through the enemies' own hidden trap.

relationship: related use of Jerusalem's gates for Sabbath regulation
rationale: Jeremiah is sent to the gates to deliver the Sabbath warning that follows. Nehemiah later stations servants at Jerusalem's gates and closes them so that Sabbath burdens will not pass through, giving a concrete counterpart to the location of Jeremiah's warning.

relationship: close royal and public summons at the gates
rationale: Both summonses address Judah's king or kings together with the people entering the gates and call them to hear the Lord's word. Their surrounding instructions differ: Sabbath observance here and royal justice in chapter 22.

relationship: close prohibition of Sabbath burdens at Jerusalem's gates
rationale: Jeremiah forbids lifting Sabbath burdens and going out through Jerusalem's gates. Nehemiah describes burdens brought into Jerusalem on the Sabbath and orders the gates guarded against their passage; the directions of movement are not identical.

relationship: explicit appeal to the inherited Sabbath command
rationale: Jeremiah commands the Sabbath's consecration and cessation from work, identifying this as what God commanded the fathers. Exodus supplies the command to keep the Sabbath holy and perform no work on it.

relationship: close hardened-neck refusal to hear inherited commandments
rationale: Jeremiah describes a neck hardened beyond the fathers and refusal to hear or accept instruction. The confession in Nehemiah likewise joins the fathers' stiffened necks with refusal to hear God's commandments.

relationship: parallel conditional blessing attached to Sabbath observance
rationale: Jeremiah introduces blessing with the condition of listening, keeping the Sabbath holy and doing no work. Isaiah likewise conditions promised good upon honoring the Sabbath and refraining from one's own wishes and work; the promised benefits are expressed differently.

relationship: close promise of Davidic kings entering with chariots and horses
rationale: Both passages promise kings seated on David's throne entering through gates with chariots and horses if the preceding divine instruction is obeyed. Jeremiah 17 names the city's gates, while chapter 22 names the royal house's gates.

relationship: related offerings brought to the Lord's house
rationale: Jeremiah foresees worshippers from Judah and surrounding districts bringing offerings and praise into the Lord's house. Isaiah promises acceptable burnt offerings and sacrifices there for the foreigners described in its context; the groups are distinct, while the temple-and-offering connection is explicit.

relationship: related warning and account of Jerusalem's burning
rationale: Jeremiah threatens unquenched fire consuming Jerusalem's quarters if Sabbath instructions are rejected. Chronicles records the burning of Jerusalem's citadels and the sanctuary, then relates the desolation to the land's Sabbaths and Jeremiah's word; it does not identify this individual warning as its sole referenced prediction.

relationship: related commands initiating pottery-based prophetic signs
rationale: God sends Jeremiah to the potter's house to hear His words; the following pottery sign begins with a command to acquire an earthenware jar and go to a specified place. The scenes use different actions and locations, while both divine instructions prepare a material sign involving pottery.

relationship: related observation of the potter at work
rationale: Jeremiah sees the potter working upon the stones. Sirach describes a potter at work turning a wheel with his feet and shaping clay with his arm; it supplies a craft parallel without equating the source's stones with an expressly named wheel.

relationship: related potter's authority to shape a vessel
rationale: Jeremiah observes the potter remaking a vessel that fell apart according to what pleased him. Romans invokes the potter's authority over a lump of clay to make different vessels; it does not narrate the collapse and remaking seen by Jeremiah.

relationship: close divine shaping of a people pictured as clay
rationale: God tells Israel that they are clay in His hands like the potter's material. Isaiah's prayer likewise calls the people clay and the work of the Lord's hands, expressly addressing Him as Father.

relationship: close divine authority to remove and destroy nations
rationale: The Lord's announced action against a nation or kingdom recalls Jeremiah's commissioning over nations and kingdoms to uproot, demolish and destroy. Chapter 18 develops the conditional response to national conduct beyond the commissioning formula.

relationship: narrative counterpart to relenting when a nation turns from evil
rationale: Jeremiah states that when a nation turns from its evils God will change His mind about the planned calamity. Jonah records Nineveh's turning from evil and God's decision not to bring the calamity He had announced.

relationship: close divine purpose to build and plant nations
rationale: The promised rebuilding and planting of a nation or kingdom repeats the constructive part of Jeremiah's commission to nations and kingdoms. The following verse in chapter 18 makes the nation's obedience consequential for that promise.

relationship: related reversal through subsequent wrongdoing
rationale: Jeremiah says a nation that does evil and refuses God's voice may lose the announced good. Ezekiel likewise says a person who trusts in his righteousness but commits lawlessness will die; the comparison distinguishes the national and individual settings.

relationship: close summons to correct ways and practices
rationale: Both addresses to Judah and Jerusalem call for changed ways and improved practices. Chapter 18 sets the summons against announced evils, while the temple address promises continued settlement if the correction is real.

relationship: close refusal expressed as following the evil heart
rationale: Jeremiah 18 reports the people's determination to follow their turnings away and what pleases each evil heart. Jeremiah 7 likewise describes refusal to listen and following the thoughts of their evil heart.

relationship: close appeal to the nations to expose Israel's extraordinary infidelity
rationale: Both challenge hearers to look among the nations for anything like Israel's conduct. Chapter 2 specifies exchanging their glory and heaven's astonishment; chapter 18 calls virgin Israel's actions horrifying.

relationship: related abandonment of the ancient paths
rationale: Jeremiah 18 combines forgotten allegiance with weakening in age-old tracks and stepping onto paths unfit for travel. Jeremiah 6 urges seeking the Lord's eternal paths and walking the good way, followed by the people's refusal.

relationship: close astonishment and hissing over a devastated place
rationale: Jeremiah predicts a ruined land that makes passersby astonished and shake their heads. The warning to Solomon similarly predicts astonishment and hissing at the Lord's house, explaining the calamity by abandonment of God.

relationship: related divine scattering expressed through wind imagery
rationale: Jeremiah compares the people's scattering before enemies to a scorching wind. Ezekiel says God will scatter a portion of Jerusalem's people to every wind; the passages share divine dispersion without making the winds' descriptions identical.

relationship: close conspiracy using the tongue as a weapon
rationale: Jeremiah's opponents devise a plan and propose striking him with the tongue. The psalm describes an evildoers' conspiracy whose sharpened tongues are like a sword and who discuss concealed traps; it does not support reversing Jeremiah's final statement that they will hear his words.

relationship: close plea that God hear the speaker's claim of right
rationale: Jeremiah asks the Lord to attend to the voice of his claim of right. The psalm similarly asks the Lord to hear righteousness and petition and to issue judgment from His presence.

relationship: close lament over evil repaid for good
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether evil should repay good and recalls interceding for his opponents. The psalm likewise laments repayment of evil for good and describes prayer, fasting and concern for those who troubled the speaker.

relationship: parallel imprecation involving widows and bereaved children
rationale: Jeremiah asks that the attackers' families suffer widowhood, childlessness and death. The psalm's imprecation likewise asks widowhood, orphanhood and destruction of children; the parallel concerns the petitions' content, not a general instruction to inflict these harms.

relationship: related judgment upon those concealing traps
rationale: Jeremiah asks for a cry in their houses and anticipates sudden robbers upon people who planned his capture and hid traps. The psalm describes an unjustly concealed trap and asks that the hidden snare catch those who set it.

relationship: parallel imprecation that sin remain before the Lord
rationale: Jeremiah asks that the opponents' injustices not be acquitted or their sins erased from before God. The psalm likewise asks that family lawlessness and sin remain remembered before the Lord rather than erased.

relationship: related material signs announcing Jerusalem's judgment
rationale: Jeremiah is commanded to obtain an earthenware jar, which the following oracle will use to depict the city's destruction. Ezekiel is commanded to take a brick, draw Jerusalem upon it and enact a siege, explicitly calling this a sign; the objects and enacted actions differ.

relationship: related prophetic judgment at the Hinnom burial site
rationale: Jeremiah is directed to the burial ground for the proclamation whose later verse names the Son of Hinnom. The earlier oracle likewise names Hinnom and announces that the place associated with burning children will become a burial place of the slain; the Charsith Gate is named only here.

relationship: close announcement that both ears will ring at divine judgment
rationale: Both divine announcements say the coming action will make both ears of everyone hearing it ring or resound. The judgments concern different settings: Judah and Jerusalem here, and Eli's house in Samuel's surrounding oracle.

relationship: close warning of ear-ringing calamity upon Jerusalem and Judah
rationale: The warning in Kings explicitly names Jerusalem and Judah and says both ears of everyone hearing will ring. It supplies a particularly close counterpart to this announcement, beyond the earlier expression in Samuel concerning another household.

relationship: historical counterpart to filling Jerusalem with innocent blood
rationale: Jeremiah accuses Judah's kings of filling the place with innocent blood. Kings specifically recounts Manasseh's pouring out innocent blood until Jerusalem was filled from end to end, alongside his leading Judah into sin.

relationship: close rejection of child-burning never commanded by God
rationale: Both condemn burning children and expressly deny that God commanded or conceived it in His heart. Chapter 19 names Baal's high places, while chapter 7 identifies Topheth's altar in the Hinnom ravine.

relationship: close renaming of Hinnom as a place of slaughter
rationale: Both announce coming days when the former name associated with Hinnom will give way to a name identifying the slaughtered. The supplied names differ in wording: Burial Ground of Slaughter here and Ravine of the Slain in chapter 7.

relationship: close judgment of corpses becoming food for birds and beasts
rationale: Both predict that the people's dead will feed the birds of heaven and beasts of the earth. Chapter 19 places this after military defeat and the collapse of Judah's and Jerusalem's counsel.

relationship: close desolation and dismayed passersby
rationale: Both portray a devastated place drawing a dismayed response from everyone passing through. Chapter 19 specifies the city and its wound; chapter 18 speaks of the land, astonishment and shaking heads.

relationship: close siege calamity of eating one's children
rationale: Jeremiah's prediction that besieged people will eat their sons and daughters directly parallels the covenant warning about consuming children under enemy-imposed distress. Jeremiah additionally names the flesh of one's neighbor.

relationship: lamented counterpart to children becoming food during calamity
rationale: Jeremiah announces children being eaten during siege. Lamentations describes famine and compassionate women boiling their children as food at the people's shattering, providing a retrospective lament alongside the covenant warning.

relationship: related breaking of pottery as an image of judgment
rationale: Jeremiah is commanded to smash the jar publicly, and the next verse interprets the act as judgment on the people and city. The psalm likewise pictures the crushing of nations as a potter's vessel; it does not depict Jeremiah's enacted sign.

relationship: close image of irreparable destruction through shattered earthenware
rationale: Jeremiah explains that people and city will be smashed like a vessel that cannot be healed again. Isaiah similarly compares judgment to an earthen vessel broken into pieces too small for useful recovery.

relationship: close condemnation of rooftop worship of heaven's host
rationale: Jeremiah identifies houses where incense was burned on rooftops to heaven's host and drink offerings were poured to foreign gods. Zephaniah's judgment upon Judah and Jerusalem likewise singles out people worshipping heaven's army on rooftops.

relationship: close prophetic proclamation in the temple courtyard
rationale: Jeremiah stands in the courtyard of the Lord's house to speak to the people after the pottery sign. The oracle in chapter 33 explicitly commands him to stand in that courtyard and deliver the Lord's words to Judeans coming to worship.

relationship: close hardened-neck refusal to hear God's words
rationale: Both connect stubbornly hardened necks with refusal to hear the divine message. Chapter 19 announces the threatened evils upon the city and its dependent settlements as the consequence.

relationship: related beating and physical confinement of proclaimed messengers
rationale: Pashhur strikes Jeremiah and places him in a trap after hearing his prophecy. Acts records Paul and Silas beaten and placed in prison with their feet in stocks; the authorities, setting and named restraint differ.

relationship: related warning and account of Judah's defeat and Babylonian captivity
rationale: Jeremiah announces death by enemy swords and deportation of Judah into Babylon's king's hands. Chronicles recounts the Chaldean king's killings and deportation of survivors to Babylon; it does not identify the fate of every friend of Pashhur.

relationship: close transfer of royal treasures to Babylon
rationale: Jeremiah announces that the city's strength, labors and royal treasures will be carried to Babylon. Chronicles records the transfer of temple vessels and treasures of the king and magnates there, supplying a concrete historical counterpart to the treasure clause.

relationship: related Babylonian doom associated with unauthorized prophecy
rationale: Pashhur and those to whom he prophesied falsehood are told they will die in Babylon. The later oracle names Ahab and Zedekiah as condemned through Babylon's king and links their fate with an oracle God did not command; the condemned people and manner of death differ.

relationship: related reproach endured in relation to God
rationale: Jeremiah addresses the Lord about being overpowered and becoming a continually mocked laughingstock. The psalm describes reproach endured on God's account and public mockery; it does not reproduce Jeremiah's charge that God deceived him.

relationship: related reproach incurred through association with God
rationale: Jeremiah says the Lord's word became reproach and derision to him. The psalm says reproaches directed at God fell upon the speaker; this comparison concerns transferred reproach and does not paraphrase Jeremiah's unusual opening as a cry against violence.

relationship: related inability to withhold prophecy after divine speech
rationale: Jeremiah describes his failed resolve to stop speaking in the Lord's name. Amos asks who will not prophesy when the Lord has spoken, expressing the compelling force of divine speech without Jeremiah's bodily fire image.

relationship: close movement from attempted silence to inward fire and speech
rationale: Jeremiah's attempted silence becomes unbearable burning in his bones. The psalm moves from guarding the mouth and remaining silent to a hot heart, kindled fire and speech; its stated concern about avoiding sin differs from Jeremiah's resolve to abandon prophecy.

relationship: close report of surrounding reproach and conspiracy against the speaker
rationale: Both speakers hear the reproach of many around them and describe people gathering or acting together against them. Jeremiah additionally records supposed friends watching for deception so they may take revenge.

relationship: parallel divine combat on behalf of a threatened speaker
rationale: Jeremiah declares that the Lord is with him like a strong fighter. The psalm petitions the Lord to make war on the speaker's attackers, take weapons and block his pursuers; one declares confidence while the other asks for such intervention.

relationship: close appeal to God's inward knowledge for vindication
rationale: Both appeals ask to see God's vengeance upon opponents because the speaker disclosed his defense or claim of right to Him. Jeremiah 20 says God understands kidneys and hearts, while chapter 11 says He tests them; the appeals preserve that verbal distinction within their close correspondence.

relationship: close praise for rescue of the poor from hostile hands
rationale: Jeremiah commands praise because the Lord rescued a poor person's life from evildoers' hands. The psalm celebrates the Lord's rescue of the poor and needy from stronger people and plunderers.

relationship: close curse upon the day of one's birth
rationale: Jeremiah curses the day his mother bore him. Job likewise curses his day and wishes the day of his birth to perish and become dark, expressing a closely related birth lament.

relationship: related reversal of the announcement of a male child's birth
rationale: Jeremiah curses the man who joyfully announced a boy's birth to his father. Job curses the night in which a male child was announced; the target of the curse is the time in Job, not the announcing person.

relationship: related comparison with cities overthrown by the Lord
rationale: Jeremiah wishes the birth-announcer to become like cities God overthrew in fury. Genesis supplies the explicit account of the Lord overthrowing Sodom and Gomorrah; Jeremiah's individual verse leaves the cities unnamed.

relationship: close wish that life had ended in the womb
rationale: Jeremiah wishes he had been killed in his mother's womb so that it became his tomb. Job asks why he did not die in the womb and compares the wished-for fate to miscarriage or infants who never saw light; Jeremiah's everlasting-conception image is distinctive.

relationship: parallel question about life given for suffering
rationale: Jeremiah asks why he emerged from the womb to experience labor, pain and shame. Job asks why light and life are given to people in bitterness and pain who long for death.

relationship: close account of Zedekiah sending Zephaniah to Jeremiah
rationale: Both reports name King Zedekiah and the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah in a delegation to Jeremiah. The other messenger differs: Pashhur here and Jehucal in chapter 44.

relationship: related royal inquiry about relief from the Babylonian siege
rationale: Zedekiah's delegation asks whether divine wonders will make Babylon's king withdraw. The later reply to a king who sent to seek the Lord rules out lasting Chaldean withdrawal and announces the city's burning.

relationship: related futility of armed resistance to the announced capture
rationale: Jeremiah 21 announces the turning of Judah's weapons into the besieged city. Chapter 44 says even surviving wounded Chaldeans would rise to burn the city; both undermine military confidence without describing identical actions upon the weapons.

relationship: close declaration that God Himself fights His disobedient people
rationale: Jeremiah says God Himself will fight the city with anger and might. Isaiah recalls the people's disobedience and says God turned hostile and Himself fought them, reversing the preceding account of His saving action.

relationship: close divine judgment by death upon people and livestock
rationale: Jeremiah announces a great death striking the city's human and animal inhabitants. Ezekiel similarly describes God sending death upon a land in wrath to destroy human beings and livestock.

relationship: related unspared judgment through death, famine and sword
rationale: Jeremiah names survivors of death, famine and sword being handed to enemies without divine sparing. Ezekiel's Jerusalem oracle likewise denies sparing and names death, famine and sword, while apportioning its judgments differently.

relationship: close setting of life and death before the hearers
rationale: Both addresses explicitly set life and death before their audience. Deuteronomy frames the choice through covenant obedience; Jeremiah immediately applies it to remaining in the city or going out to the Chaldeans.

relationship: close repeated promise of life through going out to the Chaldeans
rationale: Both announcements contrast death by sword and famine for those staying in the city with life for those going out to the Chaldeans. The life described as spoil here is called gain in chapter 45.

relationship: close prediction of capture and burning by Babylon's king
rationale: Both announce that the city will be handed over to Babylon's king and burned with fire. Jeremiah 21 expressly states God's intention of evils rather than good for the city.

relationship: close summons to Judah's royal house to hear
rationale: The brief address to the house of Judah's king is expanded in chapter 22's address to the king seated on David's throne, his household and people. Both introduce instructions about royal justice, not merely an unrelated prophetic speech formula.

relationship: parallel royal duty to judge justly and rescue the vulnerable
rationale: The house of David is commanded to set judgment straight and rescue the plundered. The psalm for Solomon asks righteous royal judgment and describes the king saving the children of the needy and humbling the false accuser.

relationship: related proud confidence that a dwelling cannot be overcome
rationale: Jeremiah confronts inhabitants who ask who could frighten them or enter their dwelling. Obadiah confronts Idumea's confidence in a lofty dwelling with God's promise to bring it down; the source's valley setting is distinct from Obadiah's height imagery.

relationship: related divine judgment pictured as consuming woodland fire
rationale: Jeremiah announces fire consuming the city's woodland and everything around it. Isaiah likewise describes a divinely sent burning that consumes woodland, forests and more, in its surrounding judgment upon arrogant power.

relationship: close summons to Judah's ruler and gate-entering people
rationale: Both call Judah's ruler or rulers and the gate-entering people to hear the Lord's word. Chapter 22 places the royal summons within an instruction on justice, whereas chapter 17 proceeds to Sabbath observance.

relationship: close protection of the newcomer, widow and orphan
rationale: Jeremiah commands the royal audience not to oppress the newcomer, orphan or widow. Exodus explicitly forbids mistreating the resident foreigner and widow or orphan, warning that God hears their distress.

relationship: parallel conditional continuance of the Davidic throne
rationale: Jeremiah promises kings seated on David's throne entering the royal house if the preceding word is carried out. God's address to Solomon likewise conditions the establishment of his royal throne upon faithful conduct and obedience.

relationship: parallel warning that disobedience brings desolation upon a house
rationale: Jeremiah warns that refusal of God's words will make the royal house desolate. The warning to Solomon says turning away will lead to the consecrated temple's rejection and public astonishment; the royal house and sanctuary must not be conflated.

relationship: related Lebanon-and-cedar imagery for Judah's royal establishment
rationale: Jeremiah addresses Judah's royal house as the head of Lebanon before announcing devastation. Ezekiel pictures an eagle taking Lebanon's cedar growth, then explicitly interprets the action as Babylon's removal of Jerusalem's king and rulers in verse 12.

relationship: related downfall of lofty power through Lebanon imagery
rationale: Jeremiah announces a destroyer cutting chosen cedars and casting them into fire. Isaiah joins the humbling of lofty figures with Lebanon's fall; it names a sword rather than Jeremiah's axe and does not supply the same burning scene.

relationship: close question by nations about the reason for devastation
rationale: Jeremiah pictures nations passing through the city and asking why the Lord treated it this way. Deuteronomy similarly pictures all nations asking why the Lord acted against the land with great anger.

relationship: close explanation of calamity through covenant abandonment and foreign worship
rationale: Both answer the preceding nations' question by naming abandonment of the Lord's covenant and service and worship of other gods. The correspondence includes both the question-and-answer setting and the specific explanation.

relationship: same-chapter explanation of mourning for the deported king
rationale: The command to weep for the one going out because he will not return is immediately grounded in the oracle about Shallum. The following verses specify his departure, death abroad and permanent loss of his homeland.

relationship: genealogical counterpart for Shallum son of Josiah
rationale: Jeremiah names Shallum as Josiah's son. Chronicles lists Salloum among Josiah's sons, providing the corresponding filial identification under the supplied spelling without independently describing his deportation.

relationship: related account of a deposed son of Josiah dying abroad
rationale: Jeremiah predicts that Shallum will die where he was deported and never see the land again. Kings records the removal to Egypt and death there of Joachas, identified in its context as a son of Josiah. This comparison concerns the royal death abroad without assuming that the supplied names are identical.

relationship: legal counterpart to the condemnation of withheld wages
rationale: Jeremiah condemns a builder who makes his neighbor work without payment. Leviticus forbids wronging or robbing the neighbor and withholding a hired worker's wages overnight.

relationship: close denunciation of laborers' withheld payment
rationale: Jeremiah denounces unpaid work used to build the ruler's house. James denounces withheld harvest wages and says the workers' cries reach the Lord; the work differs, but the unjust retention of payment is explicit in both.

relationship: related criticism surrounding elaborately finished private houses
rationale: Jeremiah describes airy upper rooms, cedar paneling and red ocher in the ruler's house, immediately after condemning its unjust construction. Haggai questions dwelling in houses with recessed ceilings while God's house lies waste; the criticized priorities and architectural details differ.

relationship: related royal responsibility for righteousness
rationale: Jeremiah's concluding judgment says doing judgment and good righteousness was better for the royal addressee. Proverbs says a righteous king raises a country while a lawless man tears it down; this comparison does not resolve Jeremiah's unusual opening about being provoked in Ahaz.

relationship: contrast concerning royal judgment for the poor
rationale: Jeremiah condemns failure to judge the cases of the lowly and poor as failure to know God. Proverbs presents the positive counterpart: a king who judges the poor in truth has an established throne.

relationship: close accusation against leaders joining greed with bloodshed
rationale: Jeremiah charges the royal addressee with greed, innocent blood and wrongdoing. Micah accuses leaders of distorted justice, building Zion with bloodshed and judging for gifts; both tie governing corruption to violent injustice.

relationship: contrast between denied and promised royal mourning
rationale: Jehoiakim is denied mourning with the cry Alas, lord. The later oracle promises Zedekiah mourning and the cry O lord, creating an explicit contrast between the announced funerary treatment of two named kings.

relationship: close prediction of Jehoiakim's dishonored discarded corpse
rationale: Jeremiah 22 predicts a donkey's burial and the corpse thrown beyond Jerusalem's gate. The later oracle about Jehoiakim likewise says his carcass will be thrown out to the day's heat and night's frost.

relationship: related lament over shattered or faithless lovers
rationale: Jeremiah's address calls for lament because all the lovers have been shattered. Lamentations describes Jerusalem without comfort among her lovers and with faithless friends turned enemies; it does not say those lovers themselves were shattered.

relationship: close longstanding refusal to hear God's voice
rationale: Jeremiah 22 describes refusal to listen as the addressee's way from youth. Chapter 7 recalls the command to hear God's voice and a continuing refusal across generations, without making the two chronological descriptions identical.

relationship: related judgment upon failed shepherds and their people
rationale: Jeremiah 22 announces that wind will shepherd the shepherds and that the lovers will be captive. Chapter 10 associates foolish shepherds who did not seek the Lord with scattering; it does not contain the same wind-as-shepherd figure.

relationship: close birth-pang imagery for impending calamity
rationale: Jeremiah compares the coming pangs of the cedar-nesting addressee to a woman giving birth. Micah addresses Zion with the same birth-pang image and expressly connects it with leaving the city for Babylon.

relationship: contrast between removal and choice under the signet image
rationale: God says He would remove Jeconiah even if he were a signet on His right hand. Haggai promises to make Zerubbabel like a signet because God has chosen him; the named recipients and directions of the image are opposite.

relationship: close threatened handover and recorded deportation of the same named king
rationale: The oracle identifies Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim and announces his delivery into feared Chaldean hands. The later vision is dated after Nebuchadnezzar deported the same explicitly named Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim to Babylon, giving the royal handover a specific narrative counterpart.

relationship: same-chapter parallel deaths abroad for differently named exiled kings
rationale: The oracle predicts that Jeconiah and his mother will die in the foreign land to which God casts them. The earlier oracle about Shallum likewise predicts death in the place of deportation. The kings are distinct, and the mother's fate is an additional feature of the Jeconiah oracle.

relationship: same-chapter parallel denial of return to an exiled king
rationale: The denial of return in the Jeconiah oracle parallels the earlier denial that Shallum will ever return or see the land again. These are separate royal oracles within the chapter, not an assumption that the kings are the same person.

relationship: close dishonor among foreign lands pictured as a useless vessel
rationale: Jeremiah compares Jeconiah, cast into an unfamiliar land, to a vessel with no use. Hosea compares Israel among the nations to a useless vessel, applying the same dishonoring image to the people rather than one king.

relationship: related direct summons to the earth to hear
rationale: Jeremiah addresses the land twice and commands it to hear the Lord's word. Moses' song likewise addresses the earth as a hearer of his words, together with heaven; the scope and repeated wording differ.

relationship: genealogical context for Jeconiah's offspring under the royal restriction
rationale: Jeremiah bars the named king's offspring from prospering on David's throne and ruling again in Judah. Matthew names Jechoniah at the Babylonian deportation and lists his offspring afterward; the genealogy does not itself say that those descendants resumed rule in Judah or resolve every implication of the oracle.

relationship: close condemnation of shepherds whose sheep are scattered
rationale: Jeremiah addresses shepherds who scatter and destroy God's sheep. Ezekiel accuses Israel's shepherds of failing to feed, heal and seek the sheep, then describes their scattering and exposure to beasts.

relationship: close divine judgment against negligent shepherds
rationale: Jeremiah says God will exact justice from shepherds who drove His sheep out and did not visit them. Ezekiel likewise declares God against the shepherds, requiring His sheep from their hands and removing their charge.

relationship: close gathering of scattered people into pasture
rationale: Jeremiah promises to receive the remnant from the lands of dispersion and establish them in pasture. Ezekiel likewise promises gathering from countries into Israel's land and good pasture, using the same restored-flock imagery.

relationship: close promise of newly appointed faithful shepherds
rationale: God promises shepherds who will tend the restored people so they no longer fear. The earlier restoration oracle promises shepherds according to God's heart who shepherd with knowledge; its emphasis is their character and understanding.

relationship: close Davidic rule characterized by righteousness and judgment
rationale: Jeremiah promises a righteous rising for David and a discerning king doing judgment and righteousness. Isaiah describes rule upon David's throne established and upheld in righteousness and judgment, with enduring peace.

relationship: related Rising imagery associated with royal rule
rationale: Jeremiah announces a righteous rising for David who reigns as king. Zechariah names a man Rising who builds the Lord's house and rules on his throne; the target adds temple building and a priest at his right hand, rather than simply repeating Jeremiah's oracle.

relationship: related restoration marked by safety for Israel
rationale: Jeremiah promises Judah's salvation and Israel's confident dwelling during the announced reign. Ezekiel promises that the restored flock will no longer be plunder and will dwell in hope without anyone terrifying them; it does not explain or replace the name Josedek.

relationship: close repeated replacement of the exodus oath formula
rationale: Both announce coming days when people will no longer invoke the Lord's life by identifying Him as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt. Their following verses replace that wording with the gathering from dispersion.

relationship: close repeated oath celebrating return from the north and other lands
rationale: Both describe the new invocation of the living Lord through His gathering Israel from the northern land and all the regions of dispersion and restoring them to their land.

relationship: related bodily trembling in a prophetic response to divine majesty
rationale: Jeremiah describes a shattered heart and shaken bones before the Lord and His glory. Habakkuk's prayer describes terror and trembling entering the bones; it does not reproduce Jeremiah's comparison to a person gripped by wine.

relationship: close mourning land and dried vegetation associated with human evil
rationale: Jeremiah 23 joins the land's mourning and dried pastures with an evil course. Jeremiah 12 explicitly asks how long the earth and field's grass will suffer because of the inhabitants' evil.

relationship: related corruption of both priestly and prophetic offices
rationale: Jeremiah identifies priest and prophet as defiled and says God saw their evils in His house. Micah accuses priests of answering for wages and prophets of divining for silver; its specified misconduct does not exhaust Jeremiah's broader accusation.

relationship: close judgment pictured as a dark and slippery way
rationale: Jeremiah announces a slippery place in darkness where the condemned will trip and fall. The psalm similarly asks that the enemies' way become darkness and a slippery path, adding pursuit by the Lord's angel.

relationship: historical counterpart to prophets serving Baal in Israel
rationale: Jeremiah condemns Samaria's prophets for prophesying through Baal and leading Israel astray. Elijah's confrontation explicitly contrasts following the Lord with following Baal and names Baal's many prophets; it does not identify every prophet in Jeremiah's accusation individually.

relationship: close accusation of strengthening evildoers against repentance
rationale: Jeremiah says Jerusalem's prophets support evil hands so no one turns from his evil way. Ezekiel likewise accuses the prophetic women of strengthening the lawless person's hands so he does not turn from evil and live.

relationship: related application of Sodom and Gomorrah to Judah's corrupt people
rationale: Jeremiah compares the prophets and Jerusalem's inhabitants to Sodom and Gomorrah. Isaiah's address against Judah and Jerusalem likewise invokes those cities and directly addresses rulers of Sodom and people of Gomorrah; the immediate groups and surrounding accusations differ.

relationship: close judgment pictured as painful food and bitter drink
rationale: Jeremiah 23 threatens the prophets with pain to eat and bitter water to drink. The earlier oracle threatens the law-abandoning people with distresses as food and gall-water as drink, repeating the paired punitive nourishment image.

relationship: close rejection of prophecy originating in the speaker's own heart
rationale: Jeremiah warns against prophetic words from the prophets' own hearts rather than the Lord's mouth. Ezekiel likewise condemns prophets speaking from their own heart while seeing nothing at all.

relationship: close deceptive assurance of peace
rationale: Jeremiah condemns prophets promising peace and freedom from evils to those rejecting the Lord and following their own wishes. Ezekiel similarly says prophets misled the people by declaring peace where there was no peace.

relationship: related access to the Lord's heavenly deliberation
rationale: Jeremiah asks who has stood in the Lord's standing place and seen or heard His word. Micaiah reports a vision of the Lord enthroned with heaven's army around Him and recounts the deliberation he heard; the narrative supplies an instance of claimed access without being quoted here verbatim.

relationship: close repeated announcement of swirling wrath upon the ungodly
rationale: Both announce anger proceeding from the Lord, describe its swirling movement and identify the ungodly as its destination. Chapter 23 also uses shaking and convulsion language.

relationship: close repeated completion of the Lord's heart's undertaking
rationale: Both say the Lord's fury will not turn back until He acts on His heart's undertaking, followed by understanding at the end of the days. The supplied pronoun changes from they in chapter 23 to you in chapter 37.

relationship: close denial that the prophets were sent by God
rationale: Jeremiah says the prophets ran though God did not send them and prophesied though He did not speak. Ezekiel similarly condemns those saying The Lord says although the Lord has not sent them.

relationship: related faithful ministry turning people from injustice
rationale: Jeremiah says prophets who truly stood before God and heard Him would have turned the people from evil practices. Malachi presents truthful priestly speech and the turning of many from injustice as the positive counterpart.

relationship: close affirmation that God is not far away
rationale: Jeremiah declares God drawing near and not far away. Paul's speech likewise says God is not far from each person and that in Him people live, move and exist; it does not turn Jeremiah's declaration into the question found in some other renderings.

relationship: related impossibility of escaping God's presence through place or darkness
rationale: Jeremiah asks whether a hidden person could escape God's sight and declares His filling heaven and earth. The psalm traces heaven, Hades, the far sea and darkness as places or conditions that cannot remove the speaker from God's presence.

relationship: close affirmation that nothing is hidden from divine sight
rationale: Jeremiah denies that someone hiding in concealed places can remain unseen by God. Hebrews says no creature is hidden and everything lies exposed to His eyes, directly matching the visibility clause rather than merely the spatial imagery.

relationship: close warning about dreams and false prophecy in God's name
rationale: Jeremiah reports prophets claiming dreams while speaking falsehood in His name. The later address to deportees warns against false prophets and dreams because the prophets speak unjust things in God's name without being sent.

relationship: close prophetic claims proceeding from one's own heart
rationale: Jeremiah identifies the wishes of the prophets' own hearts as the source of their false prophesying. Ezekiel directs an oracle against women prophesying from their own heart, specifying a group the source does not separately name.

relationship: related dreams threatening fidelity to God's commandments
rationale: Jeremiah accuses dream-telling prophets of planning forgetfulness of God's law, likening it to the fathers' forgetfulness through Baal. Deuteronomy warns against listening to a dreamer who urges service of other gods and instead commands adherence to the Lord's voice.

relationship: related distinction between wheat and chaff with different referents
rationale: Jeremiah distinguishes the truthful divine word from dreams through the question of chaff and wheat. John's announcement pictures wheat gathered and chaff burned in coming judgment; the shared separation image does not identify Jeremiah's kinds of speech with the target's judged people.

relationship: close comparison of God's words to consuming fire
rationale: Jeremiah 23 calls God's words blazing fire. The earlier oracle makes His words fire in the prophet's mouth and the people wood to be consumed, supplying an explicit application of the same image.

relationship: related force of God's word pictured through cutting
rationale: Jeremiah pairs blazing fire with an axe cutting rock. Hebrews describes God's word as sharper than a sword and penetrating inward divisions; the instruments and objects differ, and Jeremiah's axe is not replaced with a hammer.

relationship: close condemnation of false prophecy without divine commission
rationale: Both deny that God sent or commanded prophets who claim to speak for Him. Chapter 23 stresses false dreams leading the people astray, while chapter 14 lists false visions, divinations, omens and choices of the heart.

relationship: related accountability for spoken words
rationale: Jeremiah announces judgment on a person and household for using the forbidden Lord's burden expression. Jesus warns of accounting for idle words and condemnation by one's words; the target broadens the principle and does not prescribe Jeremiah's specific phrase prohibition.

relationship: related request for a truthful report of the divine word
rationale: Jeremiah prescribes asking what the Lord answered and spoke. Eli likewise asks Samuel what word was spoken to him and demands that none be concealed, followed by Samuel's complete report; the narrative does not contain the burden controversy.

relationship: related one's own words becoming the basis of adverse judgment
rationale: Jeremiah says a person's own word will become his burden after forbidding the disputed expression. Jesus likewise says people may be condemned by their own words; the comparison concerns responsibility for speech, not an identical use of the burden metaphor.

relationship: related rejection of people together with their inherited place
rationale: Jeremiah announces casting down the people along with the city God gave them and their fathers. The temple oracle likewise threatens the place given to them and their fathers and the people's removal from God's presence, denying that inherited location guarantees safety.

relationship: close enduring disgrace that will not be forgotten
rationale: Both describe dishonor whose memory will not disappear. Chapter 20 applies this to the prophet's pursuers, while chapter 23 announces it upon those implicated in the burden controversy.

relationship: close shared setting after Jeconiah and craftsmen left Jerusalem for exile
rationale: The fig vision is dated after Jeconiah and other groups, including craftsmen and prisoners, were deported from Jerusalem to Babylon. Jeremiah's letter to the Babylonian deportees is likewise situated after the departure from Jerusalem of the explicitly named King Jeconiah and groups including prisoners and craftsmen. The passages introduce different prophetic messages within this shared named setting.

relationship: related good and bad fruit imagery distinguishing human groups
rationale: Jeremiah's good and inedible figs become signs for the groups interpreted in the following oracle. Jesus contrasts good and evil fruit in a warning about recognizing false prophets; the signs serve different arguments and the target does not describe the fig baskets.

relationship: close visionary question asking Jeremiah what he sees
rationale: Both visions contain God's direct question What do you see, Jeremiah and the prophet's report of a visible object before its meaning is explained. The earlier object is a nut-wood staff, not the figs of this vision.

relationship: related divine favor toward people already dispersed from Jerusalem
rationale: Jeremiah identifies the deportees as the good figs whom God will acknowledge for good. Ezekiel counters Jerusalem's inhabitants' claim against the dispersed and promises to gather the scattered back to Israel's land; the fig symbolism is distinctive to Jeremiah.

relationship: close reversal from tearing down to building and planting
rationale: Jeremiah promises to rebuild and plant the returned deportees rather than tear down or pluck them out. The later oracle similarly contrasts God's prior watching to tear down and harm with His watching to build and plant.

relationship: close God-given heart and restored covenant relationship
rationale: Jeremiah promises a heart to know the Lord, return from the whole heart and the bond of My people and their God. Ezekiel promises a new heart and spirit enabling obedience and repeats the same people-and-God relationship.

relationship: close handing over of Zedekiah and Jerusalem's remaining people
rationale: Jeremiah's bad-fig interpretation names Zedekiah, his nobles and the remnant in Jerusalem for handing over. The earlier siege oracle likewise names Zedekiah and the city's survivors being delivered to enemies; the bad-fig oracle additionally includes people dwelling in Egypt.

relationship: close dispersion accompanied by proverbial disgrace among nations
rationale: Jeremiah announces scattering into kingdoms and becoming a reproach, parable and curse wherever driven. Deuteronomy likewise predicts removal with rulers to an unknown nation and becoming a riddle, parable and tale among the nations.

relationship: close divine judgments of famine, death and sword
rationale: Jeremiah names famine, death and sword against the condemned group until it disappears from the land. Ezekiel names those same three among four judgments against Jerusalem, adding harmful beasts and explicitly mentioning both people and livestock.
